label: FY27 Q1 (Jul–Sep 2026)
asOf: close of $192.81 on 6 Nov 2026; $195.09 before the report (4 Nov)
headline: Data-center revenue up 79% and targets raised again, but $776M of capex in one quarter turned cash flow negative: the stock is more than 50% below its June peak

points.b: AI optics carries all the growth
points.t: Datacenter & Communications rose 79% and is 82% of revenue; Industrial fell 15% and keeps shrinking. The company expects FY27 pro forma growth above 60% and a $4B quarter in FY28.
The new target is a quarter above 45% non-GAAP gross margin before the end of 2028 (40.6% now), from pricing, cost improvements and in-house 6-inch indium phosphide laser chips.
Capex was $776M this quarter (a year ago $104M), inventory rose $760M and operating cash flow was −$93M. Debt rose to about $4.0B and leverage from 0.7x to 1.1x.

reaction: Stock: closed at $169.76 the next day (5 Nov), down 13.0%, while optical peers (average of Fabrinet and Ciena) fell about 15% as the whole AI sector sold off; it rebounded 13.6% to $192.81 on 6 Nov. Consensus from Zacks: EPS $2.00, revenue about $2.32B (backed out from a 2.35% beat); next quarter revenue $2.55B, EPS $2.23.

segments.title: Segments
segments.take: All the growth came from data-center optics: transceivers, laser chips and optical switches sold to cloud companies and NVIDIA; the industrial laser business is shrinking.

rows.why: 800G/1.6T transceivers, data-center laser chips (indium phosphide EMLs, CW lasers), optical amplifiers and optical circuit switches (OCS). It signed a roughly $20B, five-year long-term agreement with a major AI company that starts contributing in early 2028, alongside its NVIDIA agreement.
Industrial lasers, optics for chip equipment and materials. Slow growth and lower margins; the company is gradually shrinking or selling parts of it.

segments.note: Revenue rose 50% y/y; excluding the divested aerospace & defense business, pro forma growth was 56%. The $20B agreement figure is the company's statement as relayed in third-party coverage.

extras.title: Where it sits in the AI loop
extras.take: Coherent makes the transceivers and laser chips that turn electrical signals between GPUs into light. The bigger the AI cluster, the less copper can carry and the more optics it needs.

items.w: Links between racks have long been optical; now links inside the rack are moving to optics too (near-packaged NPO, co-packaged CPO). The company sizes optical connectivity at about $90B by 2030, of which CPO/NPO is about $30B.
Indium phosphide capacity doubled a quarter early, but the in-house versus purchased chip mix hasn't improved in a year, so the 6-inch cost advantage is still ahead.
A five-year, roughly $20B agreement with a major AI company starts shipping in early 2028, with the customer sharing some expansion costs.
Chinese transceiver makers (Innolight, Eoptolink) are bigger and cheaper; once Marvell buys Lumentum it becomes a combined chip-plus-optics competitor.

extras.title: Where growth comes from
extras.take: Coherent grows on AI transceiver volume and the margin from its own laser chips. The real variable is whether the expansion spending turns into revenue and cash on time.

items.w: A $3B quarter by the end of FY27 and a $4B quarter in FY28, against $2.37B now. That implies FY28 revenue of roughly $14–16B.
The new target is a quarter above 45% before the end of 2028, driven by pricing, yields and the in-house laser-chip share.
Capex will keep rising, and inventory grew $760M in one quarter. Free cash flow has turned sharply negative, funded by debt and customer cost-sharing.
FY27 pro forma revenue growth above 60% (FY26 about +29%). CEO Jim Anderson, who joined in 2024, has raised targets twice.
Industry indium phosphide oversupply in 2028; Chinese price cuts; slower cloud capex or policy limits on data centers; less transceiver demand as customers adopt co-packaged optics.

valuation.take: About 29 times trailing non-GAAP earnings and about 20 times next quarter's guide annualized, with a P/S of about 4.9. Cheaper than optical peers, discounted for heavy capital needs, negative cash flow and the industrial drag.

scenarios.note: Bear: a transceiver price war and expansion delays leave FY28 only about 30% above FY27; base: hits the “$4B quarter in FY28” target; bull: the long-term deal and CPO ramp early. EPS = (revenue × non-GAAP operating margin − about $0.2B interest) × (1 − 19% tax) ÷ 205M shares. These assumptions are ours and are not forecasts.

pricezone.sub: FY28 EPS × our P/E; price at the 6 Nov close

scen.how: CPO and the long-term deal ramp early, 20x

pricezone.why: The price is slightly above the zone: buying at $193, the base case gains about 36% and the bear case loses about 28%, a reward/risk of about 1.3. At the $185 top of the zone it is about 1.7, at the $168 midpoint about 3.2, and at the $150 low end about 9.4. The multiples are below optical peers because Coherent funds its own expansion, has negative cash flow and carries a low-growth industrial business.

history.title: Against its own past
history.sub: P/S (TTM revenue, diluted shares), quarter ends; 17 quarter ends from 2022Q3 (after the name change)
history.note: About 4.9x now, twice the four-year median of about 2.3x but less than half the 10.9x of end-June. Its multiple used to be low because most revenue was industrial and materials; now more than 80% is AI optics, so a higher midpoint is reasonable. Calculated from SEC XBRL quarterly revenue, diluted shares and Nasdaq quarter-end closes.

cash.title: Non-GAAP EPS
cash.note: Operating cash flow turned negative as inventory rose $760M and receivables $260M in one quarter, while capex was more than seven times a year ago. Free cash flow was about −$870M (our calculation: operating cash flow less capex). Long-term debt rose from $3.2B to $4.0B. No dividend, and essentially no buybacks.

ret.note: Coherent pays no common dividend; the small dividend a year ago was on preferred stock (since converted or redeemed). No buybacks this quarter; all cash is going to expansion.
